Highly unlikely: Trump rules out need for renewed US war with Iran
Donald Trump said fresh strikes on Iran were highly unlikely if negotiations progressed. His remarks combined an opening for diplomacy with warnings of renewed military action.
US President Donald Trump has said it is “highly unlikely” that he would need to order fresh military strikes against Iran, provided negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear programme and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz make progress.
In a 20-minute phone interview with CNN on Sunday, Trump repeated the assessment five times, while warning that US forces were prepared to resume military action if Iran failed to agree to a strong deal.
“It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump said, adding that the US had already inflicted significant military and economic damage on Iran.
“The answer is highly unlikely it's going to be necessary. They’re a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301% inflation,” he said.
Trump also warned that Washington could deliver further military blows if required. “I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them,” he added.
US FORCES READY FOR FRESH STRIKES
Eight months after the war began, the US and Iran remain locked in a stalemate, with limited military activity and little progress in diplomatic negotiations. Meanwhile, oil tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz have faced Iranian attacks.
Trump said US forces remained prepared for renewed military action, claiming that three American aircraft carriers were deployed in the region and fully equipped for combat.
“We’re ready for it. I’ve got three aircraft carriers here. The other one just arrived. We have three. They’re fully locked and loaded,” he told CNN.
He also revealed that Washington had identified infrastructure targets inside Iran, including power plants and bridges, that could be struck if hostilities resumed.
“We have 38 bridges in our site that we can knock down in literally one hour. They’ll all be down,” Trump said.
However, he expressed reluctance to destroy Iranian infrastructure, arguing that rebuilding it could take years.
“I don’t want to do that because essentially, it’ll take 10 years to rebuild them,” he said.
DIPLOMATIC EFFORTS CONTINUE
Diplomatic activity across the Middle East has intensified since last week's US midterm elections, which were seen as a setback for Trump's Republican Party amid voter dissatisfaction over the war.
Iranian hardliners have viewed the election results as a sign of political weakness in Washington, potentially strengthening Tehran's position in negotiations.
On Friday, Qatar said Trump had spoken with Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss efforts to de-escalate tensions.
A day earlier, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held discussions with counterparts from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Pakistan, Kuwait, Jordan, Turkey, Cyprus and Qatar.
However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio played down expectations of an imminent breakthrough.
“I wouldn’t say we’re on the verge of a breakthrough,” Rubio told reporters in Florida before departing for the G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris.
He described Iran's demands as unacceptable, outrageous and unrealistic, adding that negotiations had so far failed to make meaningful progress.
TRUMP CLAIMS IRAN'S MISSILE, DRONE CAPABILITIES WEAKENED
Trump also claimed that US military strikes had destroyed Iran's air defence systems and significantly reduced its missile and drone capabilities.
According to the US President, Iran now retains just 10 per cent of its missile capacity and around 15 per cent of its drone capabilities, with much of its manufacturing infrastructure destroyed.
“The only thing they can do is about 10% level — make some missiles and make some drones. Drones at about 15% because much of their factories are gone,” he said.
Trump reiterated that he believed renewed military action would most likely not be necessary, claiming that Tehran was eager to reach an agreement with Washington.
“Most likely it will not be necessary. They want to make a deal so badly,” he said.

sources.news_title: Trump says renewed Iran strikes ‘highly unlikely’ if talks progress but warns he could still strike
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said he is "highly unlikely" to restart open war with Iran, but warned he could still strike the country as Washington tries to reach a deal with Tehran to end the conflict.
The now more than eight-month-old war, which stoked inflation and sent oil prices surging, has seen repeated bursts of fighting separated by ceasefires and peace talks for months. It was widely speculated that Trump might restart open conflict after the midterm elections, where his Republican Party lost badly to Democrats.
Trump's comments came during an interview with CNN, where he said restarting the war is unlikely as long as talks to constrain Iran's nuclear program and reopen the Strait of Hormuz make progress.
"It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement," Trump said. "The answer is highly unlikely it's going to be necessary. They're a failing nation."
Trump, however, left the door open for additional strikes if he deems it necessary. The president reiterated his threats to strike bridges and power plants in Iran if the war restarts.
"I've got three aircraft carriers here. The other one just arrived. We have three. They're fully locked and loaded," the president said. "We have 38 bridges in our site that we can knock down in literally one hour."
An end to the war and reopening of the Strait of Hormuz would likely ease oil prices, though finding a truce has proven difficult. All previous attempts to end the war and reopen the strait have been met with disappointment.
Trump is likely to come under increased pressure to end the conflict, however, now that Democrats have won control of both the House and the Senate. Some Republicans are also likely to be eager for an end to the war, given the role high gas prices played in their drubbing at the ballot box.
The president has demanded Iran fully open the Strait of Hormuz and agree to never develop a nuclear weapon as part of any deal.
Later in the day on Truth Social, Trump posted that "Task Force Iron Gate is in full force and effect in the Islamic Republic of Iran."
"Coupled with history's greatest Naval Blockade, very little gets into, or out of, Iran!" he said.
Central Command announced Task Force Iron Gate on Saturday, describing it as an initiative aimed at "preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea."
The U.S. has maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports for months.

WASHINGTON/CAIRO: US President Donald Trump on Sunday (Nov 8) said he was highly unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict progress, even as both countries reported that shipping had been hit in or near the Strait of Hormuz.
"It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement," Trump told CNN in a phone interview. "The answer is, highly unlikely it's going to be necessary."
CNN did not specify exactly what it had asked Trump, who also said that if strikes resume, the US has identified potential infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges "that we can knock down in literally one hour".
Trump had hinted at renewing major attacks on Iran after last week's US midterm elections, but there has been no sign of a large-scale US military operation. Iran has said it would respond by striking US and Israeli targets.
Iranian media suggested that explosions in southern Iran on Saturday were related to Iranian military activities rather than US strikes.
Iran's state television said officials had not confirmed any missile strikes on Iranian territory following blasts heard in several areas, including on Qeshm Island in the strait.
Both the US and Iran have continued strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, however, restricting exports of energy and other commodities vital to the world economy.
Iran's state television said the evening explosions might be related to Iranian military activity in the waterway, where Iran said two vessels had hit mines and a third had caught fire.
The US said its air force had disabled a vessel in the Gulf of Oman beyond the strait.
Tasnim news agency said two missiles had struck Qeshm Island, with no official information on possible damage. Neither Iran nor the US has commented on that report. Washington said on Nov 2 that it had struck the island in a limited defensive measure against Iranians using surface-to-air missiles against US assets.
COMMERCIAL VESSEL, OIL TANKERS HIT
Since the US and Israel began attacks on Iran in February, Tehran has sought the upper hand by hitting vessels in the Strait of Hormuz to block Gulf energy exports, while US forces began blockading movements to and from Iranian ports in April.
The US military said on Saturday evening that its air force had fired at the stern of a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, disabling it as it tried to get through the blockade.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said two oil tankers had caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to pass through an "unauthorised route" in the Strait of Hormuz. A third tanker had also suffered an explosion and caught fire, the semi-official Fars news agency reported later.
Reuters was not able to confirm any of the reported strikes.
Monitors from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said a bulk carrier and military forces were involved in an incident in the Gulf of Oman, approximately 18 nautical miles east of the United Arab Emirates' city of Khor Fakkan, with damage unknown. It was unclear if it was related to the reported US attack.
SAUDI STATE OIL COMPANY BUILDING DAMAGED
A conflict between Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia has escalated this month, enlarging the wider Middle East war.
On Sunday, Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said an administrative building belonging to state oil company Saudi Aramco in Riyadh had been damaged by falling debris after an attempted attack, with no injuries or fatalities reported.
Qatar, which has been mediating in talks to try to end the conflict that has shaken the world economy, on Saturday denied reports that the US and Iran had failed to reach a deal.
The Qatari prime minister had affirmed that both sides were continuing to work toward an agreement, it said.
Iran has submitted a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday, saying the US was reviewing it but discussions would depend on Washington first meeting Tehran's seven demands.
These include sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and war reparations, while Washington insists nuclear issues must feature in initial talks.
On Saturday, the US military said it was launching a task force to crack down on the movement of advanced weapons and other sanctioned material to Iran via its land borders and the Caspian Sea — part of economic measures to try to pressure Tehran.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards dismissed the plan as "wordplay", saying it would not work because Tehran had made preparations and communicated closely with its neighbours.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump appeared to dismiss the possibility of returning to an all-out war with Iran, telling CNN’s Jim Sciutto he believes it is “highly unlikely” as long as there is progress through negotiations.
The president said the decision to return to major military conflict between the U.S. and Iran hinges on “whether or not they sign a very strong agreement.”
“Most likely it will not be necessary,” Trump said of continued fighting. “They want to make a deal so badly.”
Trump repeatedly said Iran was “withering away” both financially and militarily on the roughly 20-minute call with Sciutto, CNN reported Sunday, but added that the U.S. forces in the Middle East are prepared to strike at any moment.

“I would, if necessary,” strike them again, Trump said, “but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them.”
U.S. and Iranian officials have not had direct talks in months after negotiations this summer failed to reach an agreement to end the war, leaving indirect negotiations as the chief method of communication between the two countries.
Iran sent a new proposal to Washington through Qatari mediators on Thursday, which included a list of seven conditions that the U.S. needs to meet before Iran will agree to any discussions. Some of Iran’s terms include lifting U.S. sanctions and war reparations, Reuters reported last week.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters Sunday that he “wouldn’t say” that the U.S. is “on the verge of a breakthrough” with Iran. He added that Trump would prefer to solve every problem diplomatically rather than through military force, but Rubio noted “sometimes that’s not possible, unfortunately.”
“Right now, it hasn’t been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous, and really not realistic,” Rubio said.
In the days after the midterms, Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have cited the Iran war as a significant factor in Democrats’ sweeping successes across the country.
Iran’s Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi urged the U.S. to accept his country’s terms and move forward with Iran’s accelerated plan to end the war, citing the American midterm results.
“American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own,” Araghchi wrote Sunday on X. “Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results.”
Trump announced a temporary pause in U.S. strikes on Iran on Oct. 8, and the ceasefire was supposed to last through the midterms — though limited, defensive strikes on Iranian targets resumed shortly before Election Day.
The brief lull in larger-scale military strikes follows several intense campaigns. U.S. forces hit Iranian targets for 13 straight nights in July and launched major attacks on Iranian facilities in September. U.S.-Iranian hostilities have persisted throughout the conflict’s fluctuations, most notably through naval blockades and exchanges of fire in the Strait of Hormuz — leading to severe spikes in global oil prices.
U.S. Central Command’s Adm. Brad Cooper unveiled the Iron Gate Task Force on Saturday to specifically reinforce “the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea.” The task force will consist of a mix of approximately 20 civilian and military personnel based in CENTCOM’s Tampa, Florida, headquarters.
Trump has repeatedly asserted that Iran must not have a nuclear weapon, and U.S. military efforts do not appear to have strayed from that course. On Friday, CENTCOM announced $20 million compensation and “possible relocation” for individuals that provide tips about Iran’s nuclear program “including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above.”
This story has been updated with a comment from Marco Rubio.

He added that the US military had 38 bridges in their sights "that we can knock down in literally one hour."

Iran and the US stuck between war and peace

The US president has since repeatedly declared victory, insinuated that Iran was begging the US for a deal, and told the media that a peace deal was done or nearly done.
Iran has repeatedly rejected Trump's account. Despite Trump's claims that Iran was collapsing both economically and militarily, Tehran has been able to repeatedly stage attacks on US allies in the region and maintains at least a partial blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthi rebels in Yemen, allied with Tehran, are currently targeting high-profile targets in the Saudi capital of Riyadh and elsewhere across Saudi Arabia.
The most tangible diplomatic achievement since the start of the war was reported in June, when Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding in Islamabad. But the talks broke down and the memorandum expired in August, with the two sides still engaged in a military and diplomatic stalemate.
Iranian top diplomat says US still digesting midterms
The conflict has proven to be unpopular with the US public, featuring heavily in the campaign for US midterm election that eventually saw Trump's Republicans lose their majorities in Congress.
On Sunday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that that peace mediators did not "travel" since the Tuesday election in the US. Araghchi described the outcome as a "shock."
"We now have to see how long it will take for them to digest these results, in order to determine how we are going to move forward," he said.
Qatar says talks moving behind the scenes
Qatar, which acts as one of the mediators in the conflict, denied rumors that the US and Iran are failing to reach a peace deal. On Saturday, the Qatari prime minister said both sides were still working toward an agreement.
Separately, the Reuters news agency cited a senior Iranian official as saying that Tehran has submitted a proposal on its nuclear program to Washington through Qatar.
The official also noted that further talks would depend on the US meeting Tehran's demands, including the lifting of sanctions, unfreezing Iranian funds and war reparations.

U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that the United States was "highly unlikely" to resume its war with Iran, citing Tehran's apparent willingness to reach an agreement, but warned that Washington had identified dozens of Iranian infrastructure targets it could destroy if hostilities resumed.
In an interview with CNN, Trump said the prospects of renewed fighting depended on progress toward an agreement, adding that Iran "want to make a deal so badly."

"I don’t want to do that because essentially, it’ll take 10 years to rebuild them," he said. "I don’t like ripping down bridges. And the hardest thing to build is a bridge. It takes years, and I’m a good builder."

"The only thing they can do is about 10% level — make some missiles and make some drones. Drones at about 15% because much of their factories are gone," Trump said.

"American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own," Araghchi said. "Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results. Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell."

The proposals are intended to bridge differences over Iran's nuclear program, which remains the most difficult issue in negotiations to end the war.
One of the officials cautioned that Iran was not yet prepared to enter negotiations with the Trump administration over its nuclear activities unless Washington first accepted several fundamental conditions Tehran wants included in any ceasefire agreement.
Trump has insisted that the nuclear dispute must be resolved as part of any broader agreement to end the fighting.
That demand has complicated diplomatic efforts, with Iran seeking guarantees on the terms of a ceasefire before committing to negotiations on its nuclear program.
A source familiar with the negotiations said Trump would prefer an agreement that would allow him to declare victory in the campaign. In addition to Qatar, Pakistan and Russia are reportedly involved in efforts to broker an agreement.
The diplomatic push comes amid growing time pressure, with some estimates suggesting Trump has roughly two months left to act until a new Democratic-led Congress is sworn in.
Despite the impasse, recent reports have suggested that the two sides may be moving closer to a breakthrough.
Bloomberg reported last week that the United States and Iran were approaching a possible diplomatic breakthrough, citing a diplomat familiar with the talks who said Tehran had shown a willingness to discuss nuclear issues it had previously refused to address.
According to the diplomat, Iran was reviewing proposals concerning its nuclear activities that had been presented by Qatar.
Any Iranian concession on those issues could produce significant progress in negotiations that have been largely stalled since the collapse of the memorandum of understanding reached in June.
The potential shift in Tehran's position has raised hopes that diplomatic efforts could succeed in resolving differences that have persisted throughout the eight-month conflict.
Despite Trump's suggestion that another round of fighting is unlikely, American military planners continue to prepare for the possibility that diplomacy will fail.
Two officials familiar with the matter told Reuters Sunday that Trump received a briefing a week and a half earlier from Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, on options for resuming military operations against Iran.
According to a U.S. intelligence official and two other senior American officials cited by Reuters, intelligence assessments conducted in recent months have concluded that renewed strikes against Iran would be unlikely to substantially alter Tehran's negotiating position.
The assessments also indicated that additional military action would not be expected to bring about the collapse of Iran's government.
The prospect of renewed fighting has also exposed deep divisions within the Trump administration, according to a senior Israeli official familiar with the deliberations.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Cooper favor resuming military operations to eliminate the Iranian threat, while Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, has taken a more cautious position.
Vice President JD Vance and advisers Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner strongly oppose renewed fighting and favor continued diplomatic negotiations, the official said.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has reportedly avoided taking a position while presenting Trump with the available options, apparently to avoid clashing with Vance. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, meanwhile, favors tightening economic pressure on Iran rather than resuming military operations.
"There is no way to know what the president will ultimately decide," the Israeli official said.
The disagreement has also spilled into the administration's assessment of last week's midterm elections. Vance has blamed the Republican defeat on the prolonged war with Iran, but Trump's polling advisers reportedly reached a different conclusion.
According to internal surveys, Republican voters who switched sides did not cite Israel or the Iran war as reasons for abandoning the party. People close to Trump also disputed Vance's emphasis on the rising cost of living, pointing to polling that reportedly found just 3% of respondents cited the issue.
The dispute may have implications for the Republican Party's 2028 presidential race. One source familiar with internal party developments said Vance had "shot himself in the foot," seriously damaging his prospects of winning the nomination, while another suggested that Rubio's chances had improved.
Israel prepares for possible return to war
Israel, which has been closely coordinating with Washington over the Iranian threat, is preparing for a range of scenarios, including the possibility that hostilities will resume.
The IDF has already begun preparations for a potential return to fighting against the Islamic Republic.
According to sources familiar with the discussions, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been pressing Trump to authorize renewed strikes, apparently hoping that a return to fighting could help break the political deadlock in Israel.
Earlier, however, Israel had sought to delay an American strike over concerns that it would disrupt the Israeli election. Officials at Israel's underground military command center reportedly debated how to persuade Trump to postpone the operation without risking the loss of an opportunity that might not arise again.
Since that postponement, Trump has reportedly set several additional dates for potential strikes against Iran, only to delay them each time.
Israeli officials have warned against attempting to predict Trump's intentions, particularly given his willingness to make unexpected decisions despite the advice of senior officials.
One senior Israeli official said Trump could disregard intelligence assessments and order additional strikes to demonstrate resolve following the Republican Party's losses in the U.S. midterm elections.
"Trump could ignore them and attack just to show that he is strong and that he doesn't care about the election results," the official said.
Israel's ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, said over the weekend that Israel would support whatever decision Washington makes regarding Iran.
Speaking in English to the Saudi-owned Al Arabiya network, Danon rejected suggestions that Israel or the United States was considering the use of nuclear weapons. "Israel will support the U.S. decision regarding Iran," Danon said. "No one in Israel or the United States is discussing the possibility of a nuclear strike."
Danon also accused Iran of continuing its pursuit of nuclear weapons despite the military campaign against it.
"Iran continues its efforts to obtain nuclear weapons and has not stopped," he said. "Israel and the United States have the technology to know what is happening in Iran."

sources.news_title: Trump Says Full-Scale Iran War Now 'Highly Unlikely' — But Mines Are Still Closing the Strait
sources.text:
The Briefing:
- Trump told CNN on Sunday that a return to full-scale war with Iran is "highly unlikely" as long as talks advance — repeating the phrase five times and saying Iran retains only 10% of its missile capacity and 15% of its drone capabilities.
- Iran's state media walked back its own reporting on Saturday's Qeshm explosions, suggesting the blasts may have been tied to Iranian military activities rather than a new U.S. strike.
- Two oil tankers caught fire after striking mines in the Strait of Hormuz, with Iran's Revolutionary Guards saying the vessels were traveling through an unauthorized corridor.
- CENTCOM announced a $20 million bounty for intelligence on Iran's nuclear program, and the Pentagon launched a new task force targeting weapons smuggling routes into Iran via land borders and the Caspian Sea.
The Iran conflict shifted register on Sunday. After days of missiles, drone claims, and disputed blasts over Qeshm Island, President Trump sat down with CNN and said — five times in 20 minutes — that a return to full-scale war with Iran was "highly unlikely." Within hours of that interview, two commercial tankers were burning in the Strait of Hormuz after striking Iranian mines. The contradiction is now the story.
Trump's Sharpest Diplomatic Signal Yet
The Sunday CNN interview with anchor Jim Sciutto marked the clearest signal yet that Trump is leaning toward a negotiated exit from the conflict. "It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement," Trump said, linking any restraint on new strikes to Iran's willingness to reach a deal covering its nuclear program and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. "They want to make a deal so badly," he added.
The conditions Trump outlined align with what Qatari mediators have been pressing for in closed-door sessions. Qatar's prime minister acknowledged the difficulty of the moment, saying no deal would be perfect but that waiting for a perfect agreement while the war grinds on was itself a failure. "Qatari mediators remain in close coordination with the United States and Iran to support ongoing negotiations," Doha said in a formal statement Friday.
Iran's core demand — that Washington meet several preconditions before any nuclear discussions can begin — remains the central obstacle. Tehran insists the U.S. must first agree to baseline concessions before its atomic activities become a negotiating topic, a position that conflicts directly with Washington's insistence that nuclear issues be addressed upfront.
What Trump Said About Iran's Military Strength
The Sunday interview carried a significant intelligence disclosure. Trump stated that Iran currently retains approximately 10% of its pre-war missile capacity and roughly 15% of its drone capabilities, citing the destruction of manufacturing facilities as the primary cause. "Drones at about 15% because much of their factories are gone," he said. If accurate, those figures represent a substantially degraded Iranian military — but also a force still capable of threatening shipping, as Sunday's events demonstrated.
By Sunday morning, Iranian state television had not confirmed any missile strikes on Iranian territory, and Iranian media suggested the southern blasts may have been connected to Iranian military activities rather than incoming fire. Reuters reported it could not independently verify any of the reported strikes from Saturday. The situation remains unresolved — but the automatic attribution of Saturday's explosions to U.S. munitions was premature.
Mines, Tankers, and a Shipping Crisis That Won't End
Whatever the source of the Qeshm blasts, the Strait of Hormuz remained actively dangerous on Sunday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy reported that two oil tankers caught fire after striking mines while attempting to navigate what Tehran described as an unauthorized passage through the strait. No casualty figures were immediately available. The incident underlines a persistent reality of this war: even during diplomatic pauses and limited strikes, the physical chokepoint through which approximately 20 million barrels of oil once flowed daily remains contested and lethally mined.
Pentagon Adds Economic and Intelligence Pressure
Alongside the diplomatic track, Washington rolled out two new pressure instruments over the weekend. CENTCOM announced a bounty program offering up to $20 million and possible relocation in exchange for actionable intelligence on Iran's nuclear infrastructure — its facilities, equipment, key personnel, and the movement of any related material. Separately, the U.S. military announced a new task force targeting weapons and sanctioned goods moving into Iran through its land borders and the Caspian Sea. Iran's Revolutionary Guards dismissed the initiative as "wordplay," saying Tehran had already prepared for such measures and coordinated closely with its neighbors.
The Midterm Reckoning and What It Changed
Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate in the November 3 midterm elections — a double loss Trump has linked directly to public exhaustion with the Iran conflict. The election result appears to have accelerated the administration's diplomatic instincts: Vice President JD Vance and envoy Steve Witkoff have internally backed deal-making, while CIA Director John Ratcliffe, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have preferred sustained economic pressure. The Sunday interview suggests Trump is, at least for now, closer to the Vance-Witkoff camp than the pressure-only bloc.
Where Things Stand
The conflict that opened on February 28, 2026 when Israel and the United States launched their initial strikes on Iran now enters its tenth month in a state of managed, low-intensity violence punctuated by high-stakes diplomacy. Trump has said major escalation is unlikely. Iran's military capacity is significantly degraded but functional. The Strait of Hormuz is mined and contested. Qatari mediators are still at the table. And both sides are insisting, with mounting frequency, that the other side wants a deal.
What nobody has yet produced is the deal itself.

Trump says a new Iran strike is highly unlikely if talks deliver a deal. But the strikes already landed this week, so is this real de-escalation or just conditional rhetoric?
President Trump told CNN that renewed strikes on Iran are highly unlikely if negotiations make progress. He repeated the phrase five times across a twenty-minute phone interview. The condition he named was blunt: Iran must sign what he called a very strong agreement covering the nuclear program and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. That is the de-escalation headline. Here is the part that complicates it.
The same administration carried out a fresh round of minor strikes on Iranian air defense systems at Qeshm Island within the last day. Reports also indicate the Pentagon has forces staged for major strikes if talks collapse. So the olive branch arrived with the artillery still warm, which is a tension markets noticed even if the headline writers did not.
For traders, the structural point matters more than the soundbite. A conditional promise not to strike is not the same as a resolved conflict. The risk premium sitting inside global markets only falls when the risk itself falls, and nothing here has removed the staged forces or reversed the Qeshm Island action.
That is why the crypto reaction was close to nothing. BTC changed hands near $75,736, down a rounding error on the day. ETH held near $2,229, equally unmoved. When a de-escalation story lands and the tape does not flinch, the market is telling you it has heard confident forecasts before.
The signal is real and worth watching. The resolution is not yet signed, and price is treating it exactly that way.
Conditional words against confirmed strikes
The transmission from Middle East tension to crypto runs through one channel: the risk premium. When conflict escalates, oil and safe havens firm, risk appetite thins, and liquidity drains from assets like BTC. A credible de-escalation reverses that, loosening the premium and freeing capital to chase risk again.
Trump's comments point that direction. A promise to hold fire, if Iran signs, lowers the probability of a Strait of Hormuz disruption and the oil shock that would follow. On its own first-order logic, that is mildly supportive for global risk and therefore for crypto.
But the signal is conditional, and the condition is unmet. There is no signed agreement. There are, instead, fresh strikes on Qeshm Island and forces staged for more. The backdrop is genuinely two-sided, not clearly improving.
That ambiguity is the whole story. A risk premium only compresses when the market believes the tail risk has shrunk. Here the dovish words and the confirmed strikes cancel out, so the premium stays roughly where it was rather than falling.
This matters because crypto trades on liquidity conditions, not press releases. Easier geopolitics would mean more risk-on flow across the board. Unresolved geopolitics means that flow stays parked. The de-escalation keyword is doing a lot of work for a situation where nothing has actually been de-escalated yet, and the market has quietly decided to wait for the paperwork.
Crypto's non-reaction tells the story
Watch what the tape did, because it did almost nothing. BTC near $75,736 printed a 24-hour move you would struggle to see without a magnifying glass. ETH near $2,229 matched the apathy. That absence of reaction is itself the signal.
In a genuine de-risking event, you expect a visible sequence. BTC catches the first bid as the headline hits, ETH follows with a slight lag, and only then does liquidity rotate down the risk curve into higher-beta alts. None of that fired here.
The reason is straightforward. The market is treating Trump's comments as conditional rhetoric, not a resolved outcome, so no one is repricing the risk premium yet. There was no rush into BTC, no follow-through into ETH, and no discernible flow into alts.
The bullish lean in this story is real but small. A credible path to de-escalation does, at the margin, support risk appetite and gently favors the upside once a deal firms. We read the direction that way on the facts.
But the near-zero price response caps how far that read travels today. Smart money is not accumulating on this headline, and retail is not distributing into it, because the catalyst has not resolved into anything you can position around. The flow will come if a signed agreement comes. Until then, this is a story the charts have politely filed under pending.
A signed deal, not a soundbite
The confirmation here is simple and binary: a signed agreement. If Iran actually signs a strong deal covering the nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz, the risk premium can genuinely fall, and that is when crypto gets a real liquidity tailwind. That is the event to trade, not the phone interview that preceded it.
The invalidation is equally clean. Renewed major strikes, or a visible breakdown in talks, would reverse the whole premise. The Pentagon's staged forces are the tell. If those move, the de-escalation narrative is gone and the risk premium widens instead of compressing.
Between those two poles sits the current reality: more of the same. Minor strikes continue, words soften, nothing resolves. In that holding pattern, expect crypto to keep ignoring the headlines and trade on its own technical structure instead.
So the practical watch list is short. First, any official confirmation that an agreement has been reached, which would be the first-order bullish trigger. Second, any escalation at Qeshm Island or beyond, the bearish trigger. Third, oil, because a real Hormuz resolution shows up there before it shows up in crypto.
And a caution worth stating plainly. This administration said strikes were highly unlikely while this week's strikes were already on the record. Confident geopolitical forecasts have a long history of ageing badly. Position for the signed document, not the promise of one, and let the tape confirm before you act.
Positioning around an unresolved Iran risk
The ParadiseTeam reads this as a headline, not a catalyst, and the levels show why. BTC was trading near $75,736 as of the print, which sits right at the $76,000 support that marks our key line. Price is leaning on that level while the Iran news passes straight through it. That is the context. A mild de-escalation signal does not change the structure here; it simply fails to rescue it either way.
Our standing map still frames the board. Whales have been net buyers into this fear, absorbing sell pressure rather than chasing, with the Fear and Greed read near 20. Reclaiming $76,000 and holding it keeps a short-term squeeze toward the $81,700 to $82,500 cluster in play, where roughly 2.2 billion in shorts sit as fuel.
Lose $76,000 cleanly, though, and the $70,000 to $71,000 band comes into focus as the next magnet. A geopolitical de-escalation that never gets signed will not stop that.
So we treat any strength on this story as potential relief, not a trend change. Our dominant daily and weekly bias stays cautious toward lower targets until invalidated. Over-leveraged shorts into resistance can still get hunted on an upside squeeze, which is the real risk for the bearish crowd. The honest position: do not trade the soundbite. Trade the signed deal if it ever arrives, and let $76,000 tell you who is winning in the meantime.
